articles.title_orig: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.title_zh: Kim Jong Un Remakes North Korea’s Flag, Ditching Soviet-Era Version
articles.content_orig:
SEOUL, Nov. 13 (Yonhap) -- North Korea has revised its constitution to change its national flag's aspect ratio for the first time since its regime was established in 1948, according to the amended basic law posted on the website of Pyongyang's propaganda outlet.
Article 166 of the revised constitution posted on Naenara's website stipulates that the ratio of the flag's height to its width is 1 to 1.65, replacing the previous ratio of 1 to 2.
The change came as North Korean leader Kim Jong-un has sought to build his own governing style and national identity while retaining some legacies of his predecessors.
The flag's 1-to-2 ratio rule had remained unchanged in the law until the North's constitutional revision in September 2023.
Despite the ratio change, the overall design of the North's flag remains intact, consisting of a broad red stripe in the center, narrow white stripes above and below it, blue stripes above and below the white stripes, and a red five-pointed star in a white circle.
The constitution says the red stripe stands for the blood shed by anti-Japan fighters who dedicated their lives to defending the country's freedom and independence during Japan's 1910-45 colonial rule. The white circle and two white stripes symbolize people's loyalty to the nation's leader and ruling Workers' Party of Korea.
The two blue stripes represent the revolutionary spirit of the people struggling for peace, friendship and unity in the world, as well as the country's sovereignty, it said.
Observers said the change in the flag's aspect ratio might have reflected Pyongyang's efforts to craft a new national image under the incumbent leader Kim, the third-generation hereditary ruler.
This image, captured from the website of North Korea's propaganda outlet Naenara, shows the North's revised constitution. (PHOTO NOT FOR SALE) (Yonhap)

I t’s beginning to look a lot like 2017, thanks to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
The Nvidia co-founder’s career has spontaneously combusted since he admitted last week to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials suspect of being an asset or agent of China’s Ministry of State Security, its equivalent of the CIA.
A trio of House committee chairs have demanded Huang appear before Congress to brief them on his ties to Ms. Huang (no relation).
On Monday, The New York Times revealed that he’d also had a second affair with one of his subordinates, leading Nvidia’s board to move towards tossing him out of the company he’d started three decades earlier.
The tech billionaire’s problems have brought about a temporal vibe shift — reviving and exposing Trump administration infighting and leaking at a level not seen since the heady early months of the president’s chaotic first White House term.
To start, the Times scooped that Marco Rubio, Secretary of State cum National Security Adviser, was so sufficiently alarmed at what U.S. intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum detailing how she’d allegedly been recruited by the Chinese spy agency.
The goal of the Chinese operation was reportedly to send Alice Huang to target Jensen Huang in hopes of learning more about his products and influencing him to push Nvidia towards selling Beijing more of the company’s cutting-edge AI chips, according to reports.
Rubio was so concerned by what he read about the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang that he made a point of briefing President Donald Trump on the memorandum while aboard Air Force One en route to China this past May.
Yet the Secretary of State’s warnings appeared to have little effect on Trump. He was so hell-bent on having Huang travel with him to Beijing that he ordered his Air Force One crew to wait at an Alaska air base for Huang to meet him there on a private jet.
Trump appeared to have been taken in by a charm offensive the then-Nvidia CEO was mounting to convince him to relax export controls on his company’s top-end chips.
The Biden administration had restricted their export out of concern that acquiring them could help foreign adversaries (mainly Beijing) gain an advantage over the U.S. in the race to develop the most advanced AI models.
Huang’s effort was incredibly successful.
Having curried favor with the president by way of a $25 million corporate donation to the controversial White House ballroom project, Trump and his allies began giving Huang a freer hand in who he sold his products to. In turn, Huang became a frequent visitor to the White House.
At the same time, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — the U.S. official responsible for administering the country’s export control regime — was reportedly refusing to impose any sanctions on Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, despite serious concerns from the U.S. intelligence community over whether the company was serving as a front for Beijing’s efforts to acquire more of Nvidia’s top-end products.
Now, with Huang having been forcibly exited from the empire he built, the scrutiny is intensifying on Lutnick.
Administration officials have always been reluctant to so much as hint at criticizing Trump, and his cozy relationship and seeming willful ignorance of Jensen Huang’s dalliance with an alleged Chinese honeypot is no exception.
But the Commerce Secretary, a longtime friend of Trump’s going back to their days as New York City high-rollers, does not inspire the same fear.
Newly resurfaced audio, from the tech bro favorite All In podcast, reveals him boasting about his own close relationship with Huang, who he called a “national treasure” that he had brought into Trump’s inner circle.
“I promised him in the beginning when I first met him that I would help him have really easy access to the president,” Lutnick said during a podcast taping in January, speaking to a cohort of hosts that included the then-White House AI Czar, David Sacks.
He described how Huang sold Trump on relaxing export controls by arguing that it would keep China dependent on his own AI chips rather than building up domestic manufacturing, and said Trump agreed with the caveat that Nvidia pay a 25 percent tariff when importing them into the U.S. for testing.
“He (Huang) has to send the chips to America. We test the chip to make sure that he hasn’t enhanced it in any way... On the way in, we can charge it a tariff, a regular 25 percent tariff, and then we can give export licenses to whoever he wants to sell it to. He sends it to China, or he sends it to whoever he’s selling it to,” Lutnick said.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wasted no time pointing the finger Friday when he told CNBC that it was the Lutnick-led Commerce Department who resisted putting Megaspeed, the China-linked company, on his department’s “Entity List” of companies not allowed to purchase American products.
Asked whether the Trump administration considered adding Megaspeed to the list, Bessent replied: “I can tell you there was coordination. It was Treasury, War, [the U.S. trade representative], and State. They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen.”
Then, he twisted the knife.
“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he said.
More embarrassment for Lutnick came in the form of a leak to Axios revealing that he’d been one of the officials who’d received the Rubio memorandum warning about Jensen Huang’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed.
And things may get worse. Lutnick is scheduled to testify before Congress on this very matter within days.
Last time he was on Capitol Hill, he gave a questionable performance under questioning about his relationship with deceased sex abuser Jeffrey Epstein.
This time, he will have to explain why he didn’t care that one of America’s most important companies was selling sensitive products to a company with suspected links to Chinese espionage.

articles.title_orig: Disruptions Persist as Air Travel Recovers from Nationwide Ground Stop: Live Updates
articles.title_zh: Disruptions Persist as Air Travel Recovers from Nationwide Ground Stop: Live Updates
articles.content_orig:
Federal airspace is operating as normal after a nationwide ground stop on all departing U.S. flights threw the aviation industry into turmoil on Friday. Officials said the issue stemmed from a "telecommunication outage."
Airspace was reopened at 8:15 p.m. Eastern time, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said during a news briefing Friday night. Resumption of flight traffic was "going to be slow," Duffy warned.
In a social media post following Duffy's briefing, the Federal Aviation Administration said that "before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable."
As of 7:30 a.m. ET on Saturday, the airspace was operating as normal and being closely tracked, senior government sources familiar with the situation told CBS News.
The FAA had issued the ground stop on all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety." The ground stop lasted about five hours. There were more than 10,000 delays and over 4,000 cancellations listed Friday, according to the flight tracking website FlightAware.
There were already over 3,500 residual cancellations in the U.S. on Saturday as of 8:15 a.m. ET, according to FlightAware. Delta Air Lines led the way with 640 cancellations, while United had 530 and American had 488. Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport, Chicago O'Hare International Airport and New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport were most affected by the cancellations on Saturday morning. There were also about 1,400 flights delayed.
Duffy said Friday that routers became overloaded with data and began to provide inconsistent information.
"Because of that, we shut the system down," Duffy said, noting the air traffic control system is "incredibly old."
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in Friday's briefing that new security patches introduced into the older system appeared to "overwhelm" its routers.
The FAA's preliminary investigation has led the agency to believe the issue was limited to Cisco 600 series routers that were manufactured between 2001 and 2006, senior government sources told CBS News. The sources said the faulty equipment has been identified and isolated.
The sources said the routers essentially got overwhelmed, and started feeding out-of-sync data packets into the larger air traffic control system. That causes static over voice communication lines and can cause screens to flash or go to black.
Sources told CBS News they are receiving conflicting information about the cause of the issue. Multiple sources said Friday that an update to the the private communications network that connects the U.S. air traffic control system caused the system to reboot, leading to a crash and a communications outage.
The FAA Telecommunications Infrastructure, known as FTI, is the communications backbone that connects air traffic control centers and other FAA facilities. It supports the transmission of essential voice communications and operational data used to manage air traffic. The system is operated by L3Harris, which did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.
The FAA awarded Harris Corp., the predecessor to L3Harris, a contract to modernize, operate and manage the network in July 2002.
A November 2023 FAA-commissioned safety review described the FTI network as obsolete and said it depended on an older communications technology known as TDM.
The review also warned that the technology was no longer supported by the telecommunications infrastructure on which it relied and that an unexpected failure could leave individual FAA facilities, or even an entire regional air traffic control center, disconnected from the broader network.
There has been frustration with the L3Harris's communication and response, sources told CBS News.
On Friday night, Duffy renewed his call for Congress to approve emergency funding to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.
"But you will have more of these," Duffy said during the news conference. "You will have more of them unless the American people and the Congress tell us to build."
Mullin argued that the incident demonstrated why he believed piecemeal modernization was insufficient and said the Trump administration wants a complete replacement of the air traffic control system, at an estimated cost of $50 billion.
Mullin told reporters in an earlier briefing outside the White House Friday that "there was no indication, as of yet, that this was a nefarious act against us. It was just a telecommunication outage, as of right now."
"There is no indication, we had no reason to believe, that as of right now, that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin said. "This was a telecommunication outage throughout FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights. And all the flights are accounted for."
Mullin reiterated Friday night that there was no cyberattack and the ground stop was not related to the massive global Microsoft outage .
"I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft," Mullin said during the news briefing with Duffy. "I know a lot of people are making that jump. This is so far what we've seen. There is actually no cyberattack. We're still working through that process."
According to the flight tracking site Flightradar24 , there were about 3,100 airborne aircraft bound for U.S. airports when the ground stop began. Planes were able to land safely, Mullin said, but with no aircraft able to take off again, delays began piling up at major airports across the country in Boston , Atlanta , Miami , Pittsburgh , New York City , Los Angeles and Baltimore .
"This is absolutely unprecedented," said Robert Sumwalt, a former chair of the National Transportation Safety Board and a CBS News transportation safety expert. "I was an airline pilot for 24 years. I was in the air on 9/11. That was the last major ground stop. There was one back in 2023 for just a few hours. This is absolutely unbelievable that this could happen in this day and age."
Overall, 9,159 flights were cancelled and 7,190 were delayed, according to FlightAware. It was the second-worst travel day for airlines this year: A massive snowstorm on Jan. 25, 2026 led to 11,607 flight cancellations.
Duffy said the FAA would try to move as many flights as possible Friday night depending on crew capacity.
"If not, we're going to start tomorrow [Saturday] morning with our airline partners moving those aircraft. But it's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Duffy said he thinks flights will be "back up and operational as we come into the heat of travel" during the Thanksgiving holiday later this month.
In January 2023, a nationwide ground stop was ordered for a few hours, and domestic flights were delayed nationwide due to an FAA system outage. The FAA said at the time that its flight personnel alert system went down overnight.
Olivia  Rinaldi , Pat  Milton , Kris  Van Cleave and Sarah N. Lynch contributed to this report.

articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
WASHINGTON — In the final days before an election that will decide control of Congress, President Trump’s closing argument — buoyant, digressive and characteristically off-script — is at times running headlong into the economic anxieties of the voters Republicans most need.
With a war in Iran driving up gas prices for Americans, Trump is boasting to supporters that the conflict is making the country rich. At a rally in Georgia, he said his aides had urged him not to brag about the billions of dollars the United States was earning on oil from the war, since Americans are “paying a little higher” in costs because of it. But he did it anyway.
“I said, I don’t give a damn,” Trump said. “We are making a freaking fortune. Our country is getting stronger and stronger all the time. And those pump prices are going to come down.”
The moment underscores the gamble at the core of Trump’s final pitch to voters. With polls showing an overwhelming majority of Americans unhappy with the economy, the president is offering a portrait of national prosperity that many voters do not recognize, and pairing it with jokes and digressions that can seem to make light of their struggles.
Tuesday’s results will be the clearest test yet of whether that message still moves his base, or whether the president has become a liability for a party at risk of losing Congress in part because of his sinking popularity.
Signs of GOP anxiety are reflected in where Trump is spending his final days campaigning. Rather than courting swing voters in battleground states, he is leading rallies in Mississippi, Texas, Ohio, South Carolina and Kansas — states that have long been Republican strongholds but where the party now worries its voters may stay home.
Still, the president is insisting to voters that the country is succeeding, and he is  making the election a referendum on his agenda.
“The world is falling apart, and we are doing better than we’ve ever done,” he told a crowd in Mississippi on Monday. The next day, during a stop in Texas, he joked that the $5,000 he has promised Americans if Republicans win would not be enough for his supporters to eat a meal at Mar-a-Lago, his private club in Palm Beach, Fla.
Michigan’s Senate race has become a battle over Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. He is embracing his role as a Republican target, while consistently promoting a progressive agenda to address voters’ economic worries.
“You will be my guest at Mar-a-Lago. The problem is that for $5,000 the most you’ll be able to buy is a hamburger and maybe a small dessert,” Trump said, laughing. “I’m not even sure you could buy that.”
Democrats have criticized the president’s remarks, calling them dismissive of voters’ concerns. Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) said Trump boasting that the country was making money out of the Iran war was a “fitting” slogan for Trump’s White House.
Trump’s personal oil and gas holdings are now estimated to be worth between $22.5 million and $81.6 million , up from $12.6 million to $46 million at the end of last year, according to a report released this week by congressional Democrats.
Joe Gruters, the chairman of the Republican National Committee, rejected the idea that the president has dismissed voters’ financial pain.
“The president, I think, shows empathy about what we’re going through, and he is fighting like hell,” Gruters said in an interview.
Asked to sum up Trump’s closing message, Gruters framed it as a choice between “common sense vs. crazy.” When pressed on the economy, Gruters pointed to Trump’s push to limit federal taxes on tips and overtime pay, to create investment accounts for children and to bring back manufacturing jobs.
“He has transformed the Republican Party into the workingman’s party,” Gruters said. “He is all about trying to bring back jobs that will bring up real wages across the board.”
But that message can  be overshadowed with the off-script riffs that have long defined Trump’s rallies. During a rally in Ohio, while praising Sen. Jon Husted, Trump detoured into remarks about the Republican senator’s backside as well as rapper Nicki Minaj’s.
“I looked at his ass and I’ve never done that with a man before. It’s true. Off the record: Women, yes, men, no, OK?” Trump said. “By the way, I looked at one hell of a beautiful ass before, Nicki Minaj.”
At a separate rally, Trump turned his attention to Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic Senate nominee in Michigan, saying that if elected, El-Sayed should be forced to pass through a metal detector before entering the U.S. Senate chamber.
“Anyone with that record of support for jihadists would be screened and unable to get a seat on an airplane,” Trump said of El-Sayed. “They certainly should not give him a seat in the United States Senate.”
In those moments, the message is aimed squarely at his base, which over the last decade has celebrated his unfiltered style. And it is that base, more than swing voters, that Trump has spent his precious time courting in the final stretch of the campaign.
On Monday, Trump rallied supporters in Mississippi, a state he carried by 23 points two years ago. On Tuesday, he went to Texas for the fourth time this month to make the case for Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate nominee trying to stave off what could be the first statewide Democratic victory there in three decades. Then on Wednesday, Trump was in Ohio for the third time this month, playing defense in a state he has won every time he’s been on the ballot. And on Saturday, Trump is heading to Kansas, a state that has not elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since 1932.
Gruters said the red state swing reflects the need to get Republicans to the polls.
“You can’t take anything for granted. You have to fight hard in every single state, and remind people why they need to go vote,” he said. “This is a turnout, turnout, turnout race. And we’re doing everything we can as a party.”
Trump is rallying in Republican strongholds such as Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama, betting that his presence will be enough to energize voters who might be thinking of sitting out the election.
Don Haider-Markel, a political science professor at the University of Kansas, said it is still surprising to see the party deploy the president in Republican strongholds so close to the election.
“It really reflects, not just the tilt toward Democrats, but also the lack of enthusiasm among Republican voters for this election,” Haider-Markel said.
Republicans outnumber Democrats in Kansas, but there is a possibility that Democrats can win if Republicans stay home, he said. One of the biggest assets the party has to mobilize the MAGA base is having Trump talk to them in person, he argued. But so far, it is unclear whether his closing message will resonate.
“I don’t think that he’s really speaking to the issues that voters care about, but I don’t think he’s coming to change people’s minds,” Haider-Markel said. “He’s looking for lines that get him applause and praise.”
In rally after rally, Trump has turned the event into a show about himself. In Iowa, congressional candidate Joe Mitchell presented Trump with a “man of the century” certificate. In Texas, Trump bemoaned that he was not awarded the Nobel Peace Prize last year. And in several events, he has shown the crowd a video of a CNN analyst saying that among GOP voters, Trump is more popular than Ronald Reagan or Abraham Lincoln.
But in the end, he also tried to appeal to his base with nostalgia.
“We’ve been doing this together for 11 years, and there’s never been anything like it and there probably never will be anything like it again politically or otherwise,” he said. “So let’s go out and do what we do best and that is win on Nov. 3. We gotta win!”

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: 3 oil tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: 3 oil tankers hit mines in Strait of Hormuz, Iran says
articles.content_orig:
At least 25 seafarers have been killed in and around the Strait of Hormuz since the US-Israeli war on Iran broke out in February, according to the United Nations.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, gave the figures , which cover the period up to November 11, during a UN Security Council briefing on Friday.
“This situation cannot be allowed to become the new normal,” said Khiari, urging the “full restoration of maritime navigation in the region”.
He pointed out that security incidents in and around Hormuz have been rising, with October recording the highest tally since the start of the conflict.
The UN’s International Maritime Organization (IMO) tracked 136 security incidents involving vessels in Hormuz and the wider Middle East between March 1 and November 11. It said 35 of those incidents came in October and 10 in November.
“Every day brings new reports of maritime incidents,” said Khiari. “These incidents are unacceptable,” he added. “Civilian vessels and commercial shipping must not become targets.”
His remarks come as Iranian authorities on Saturday reported that three oil tankers had hit mines while travelling through “unauthorised” or “restricted” areas of Hormuz, catching fire.
Tehran has warned vessels that they must receive Iranian approval to cross the waterway during the conflict, and has repeatedly attacked ships accused of violating its protocol.
“Any offending tanker that travels in the restricted area east of the Strait of Hormuz will be set on fire by hitting naval mines,” Iran’s navy warned in a statement carried by the country’s IRIB broadcaster.
Iranian officials have insisted the strait will not be open until the US meets its demands , which include an end to the US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, the lifting of economic sanctions, the release of Iranian frozen funds, ending fighting on all fronts, and an explicit announcement of an end to the war.
The US military claims it has cleared the strait’s main routes of mines and that the waterway is open for commercial shipping.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz is approximately 65 percent below pre-war levels, according to the latest report from the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).
Khiari, in his remarks to the UN Security Council, said “the present maritime arrangements in the Middle East remain costly, unpredictable, and unsafe”.
“Disruptions to maritime navigation continue to have significant global economic consequences, driving up energy, transport and insurance costs, fuelling inflation and threatening food security amid severely constrained fertiliser shipments.”

articles.title_orig: Software company with thousands of Fortune 500 clients joins Microsoft in experiencing major outage
articles.title_zh: Software company with thousands of Fortune 500 clients joins Microsoft in experiencing major outage
articles.content_orig:
Microsoft said early Saturday it had restored its services after a worldwide outage which involved services like Outlook and Teams impacted users, companies and government operations around the world.
In a post on X , the company said: "We have completed our efforts to address the underlying issue of the incident and restored service to the remaining impacted customers and regions."
The disruption, which lasted over 24 hours, affected a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.
Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity, and apologised for the incident.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," the company said Friday on X . "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those tailored for personal use by individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.
"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."
Charles Lamanna, executive vice president of Copilot, Agents, and Platform at Microsoft, said in a social media post Friday that "technical challenges and failure modes" made the recovery process "more difficult than normal."
"I'm working closely with the engineering team to complete the full post-mortem," Lamanna said in the post. "We will publish the post-mortem shortly covering the step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future."
Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. ET Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account .
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social media users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. More than 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday that Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024 .
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.
"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.
Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.
Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, it could "impact the production timeline," he said.
Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.
IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage had affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

articles.title_zh: SpaceX Starship Flight 15 live updates: Starship heat shield looks good for landing attempt today
articles.content_orig:
The Starship rocket launched successfully on Friday
SpaceX will decide later whether to try to catch the top part of its huge Starship rocket as it returns to Earth.
The company had hoped to catch both the bottom and upper stages of the rocket using mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower.
But the first catch of the rocket's booster was aborted a few minutes after the launch, and instead the booster diverted to the ocean, bursting into flames just above the sea.
The top part, known as the Ship, is due to return to Earth at about 1515 local time (2115GMT) on Saturday.
This is the 15th test of Starship and the first that hoped to fully recover both parts of the rocket. SpaceX wants to make the top and bottom sections of Starship fully reusable so it can fly repeatedly and reduce costs.
The 124m-tall (407ft) rocket successfully blasted off from the Starbase launchpad in Boca Chica, Texas at 1647 local time (2147GMT) on Friday.
The plan was to grab the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - six and a half minutes later when it returned.
A "go" was initially given by mission control for a catch attempt at the launch tower, but the booster activated an automated abort, diverting instead to the ocean where it hovered above the water before exploding.
The lower stage of the rocket was diverted to the ocean and burst into flames
During a livestream of the launch, a SpaceX spokesperson said: "Safety is always the number one priority and we're still testing out things that we haven't done before on these vehicles, and so we are prioritising making sure that we can perform each manoeuvre safely."
The top part of the rocket continued its journey to space where it deployed 26 satellites, which form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high-speed internet.
The Ship is due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning to the launch tower 22.5 hours after taking off.
SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the "chopsticks".
Before the flight, SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it was in space.
If any problems are detected, there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
A SpaceX lander could take astronauts down to the surface of the Moon
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.
In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than 100 times a year and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.
But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, president of Royal Aeronautical Society.
"Full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.
"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."
After SpaceX became a public company earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will Nasa.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
What is Nasa's Artemis III mission? And what comes next?
Watch: From launch to fiery splashdown, SpaceX's Starship completes orbit test
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.
But it is not the only company working with Nasa. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touchdown.
Both companies will also play a key role in the Artemis III mission, which is currently planned for summer 2027 - another challenging schedule.
Four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft will attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers during the voyage.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said its spacecraft would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.
Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said the US was in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

articles.title_orig: Shenzhen is transforming into a heavily secured diplomatic stage for an APEC summit attended by Xi, Trump and Putin
articles.title_zh: Shenzhen is transforming into a heavily secured diplomatic stage for an APEC summit attended by Xi, Trump and Putin
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump will meet with the leaders of China and Russia on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzen , China’s tech hub, next week, an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world’s biggest nuclear powers.
“President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People’s Republic of China and the president of the Russian Federation,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, said in a call with reporters Friday night. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous.”
It is not anticipated that any sort of agreement will come from the trilateral meeting, according to a senior U.S. official, who described the session as an “entry point” and “the first conversation,” pointing to the reduction of nuclear arsenals as a key topic.
“We do think it’s time for China to sort of step up, you know, to the adults’ table, if you will, and have adult conversations about adult things,” the senior U.S. official said about the issue of nuclear weapons.
Beijing’s arsenal of more than 600 warheads , according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.
The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for “a new, improved and modernized” deal that includes China.
The three-way summit with Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin comes at a complicated moment in relations for the three countries.
Trump intends to discuss the Iran war with the two leaders, but not the war in Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that discussions about the war in Ukraine are a separate “track” that China is not part of so it would not be “appropriate.”
Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world’s foremost economic powers.
Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin , even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.
There is no bilateral with Putin scheduled, but the two leaders will appear at events and the trilateral meeting together, according to a senior U.S. official.
There are no plans for Trump to engage with North Korea during the trip, according to a senior U.S. official.
Separately, Elon Musk will be the only business leader who is part of the president’s delegation, according to a senior U.S. official, who noted that other U.S. business leaders will attend the summit in their own capacity but there is no official U.S. business delegation.
Musk will not be part of any official meetings, according to a senior U.S. official.
Two senior U.S. officials said that they don’t think Trump will raise the espionage investigation focused on Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence agent who allegedly had a romantic relationship with Nvidia chief Jensen Huang, with China.
“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip. In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls,” a senior U.S. official said. “These are national security matters that we develop in the administration and interagency process, and we don’t expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we’re there.”
By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China’s growing clout and prestige.
For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.
“I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they’re making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don’t like,” said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.
More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China’s argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia’s war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.
The trilateral meeting could undercut China’s push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.
“You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism ,” he said.
Putin and Xi are no strangers. They’ve fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as “dear friend.”
Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.
Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.
As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia , China increased its purchases of Russia’s energy resources and became Moscow’s principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.
In the lead-up to Russia’s war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a “no-limits friendship.” China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv’s Western allies played a part in provoking Russia’s military action in Ukraine .
Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing’s policy on issues related to Taiwan.
Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine’s attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv’s back.
Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can’t be enforced on others.

articles.title_orig: Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expect
articles.title_zh: Trump-Xi-Putin trilateral meeting at APEC: What to expect
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump, China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin will hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in China’s Shenzhen, the White House has confirmed .
On Friday, Washington also confirmed Trump’s attendance at the summit, which will take place from November 18-19.
Talks will focus on nuclear proliferation, the White House said. But they come amid significant global turbulence: Russia’s war in Ukraine, the US-Israeli war on Iran and ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Beijing.
“I think what we’ll see is some pretty impressive photo-ops with a lot of really bombastic rhetoric from Trump,” Simon Mabon, a professor of international politics at the UK’s Lancaster University, told Al Jazeera. However, he added, the three “collectively or unilaterally, are not able to bring about an end to the conflict in Iran or Ukraine”.
So what does each side want and what will be the likely outcome?
Each leader has his own priorities, but there are some issues all will want to discuss.
A top issue for Russia and the US is the New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START), which lapsed in February. The treaty was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.
Russia currently possesses the largest number of warheads, followed by the US and then China, which is rapidly building up its own arsenal.
Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing.
China is understood, however, to be reluctant to join an agreement it was not involved in forming.
A senior Trump administration official told Reuters this topic will start the conversation but that “we do not expect to get any kind of agreement”.
Officials also say the world leaders will discuss the Iran war , which the US and Israel launched on February 28. While full-scale strikes have, for now, ceased, the conflict remains in a deadlock .
After more than 100 days, the critical Strait of Hormuz remains closed, and oil and gas prices are still volatile as ships in the strait continue to face Iranian strikes and seamines. One-third of China’s crude oil supply transited the strait before the war. The conflict is also hampering demand for Chinese exports.
Russia, meanwhile, has profited from rising energy prices and recent sanctions relief from Washington amid supply crunches – particularly of diesel.
Trade wars and the race to control microchips used to power artificial intelligence are straining relations between Beijing and Washington.
Trump hit China with a 145 percent tax hike last year, while Beijing retaliated by imposing 125 percent levies on US imports. Tensions mounted further over China’s restrictions on exports of rare earth minerals needed to manufacture advanced chips and other technology.
The two countries have since reduced tariffs and struck several deals following Trump and Xi’s meetings in South Korea and Washington However, the recent scandal at chip firm Nvidia has prompted the US to allege that China was spying on CEO Jensen Huang. Beijing denies this.
It is very unlikely. A Trump administration official told reporters the US president will not bring up Russia’s war on Ukraine, although Kremlin officials previously suggested the conflict could be discussed.
China, an ally of Moscow’s, has said the Ukraine war is a European issue.
US officials also note that Washington is pursuing peace talks, with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visiting both Ukraine and Russia this week. “China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn’t seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there,” an official told reporters.
President Trump has accused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of “not wanting” to end the war, while Kyiv has reiterated allegations that the US has restricted its Starlink satellite connection that allows it to operate attack drones. Trump has also blamed Ukraine for soaring diesel prices because of its strikes on Russian oil facilities.
At the same time, Trump has feted Putin, agreed to allow Russian diesel into global and US markets, and lifted oil sanctions on Moscow.
For President Putin, the meeting could provide a positive photo opportunity and a platform to project power while sidelining the Ukraine conflict, analysts say.
It will give him a “first among equals” position that he can display at home to show that he can influence Europe’s security architecture following the Ukraine war, Alexander Bratersky, a Moscow-based journalist and political analyst, told Al Jazeera.
Beijing has already been pushing for a resolution to the US war on Iran, which has impacted its own energy supplies.
China will also want to avoid being pulled into a nuclear treaty it had no part in establishing.
Last month, China’s Foreign Ministry said it would be “neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.
Trump’s priority is to include both China and Russia in a new nuclear proliferation treaty, according to administration officials. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesperson, told reporters.
The president could also use the meeting to project his administration’s diplomatic influence, as Iran refuses to capitulate to US demands for ending the war and hand Washington a win.
Trump has also sought closer ties with Xi, Putin and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un, all seen as “strongmen”, and is likely to be perceived as influential in such circles, analysts say.
“I think it will be more performative – Donald Trump playing global statesman rather than peacemaker,” said Mabon.
Trump’s Republican Party’s crushing defeat in midterm elections last week could undermine his leverage, experts note, as a new Democrat-led Congress is likely to support Ukraine more staunchly.
Pyotr Tolstoy, chairman of the Russian parliament’s foreign affairs committee said it could lead to a “new Yalta”.
The 1945 conference in Yalta, in the then Soviet Union, saw USSR President Joseph Stalin, the US’s Franklin D Roosevelt, and the United Kingdom’s Winston Churchill divide Germany and establish the United Nations in what was seen as the template for a new world order.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, called the trilateral meeting now taking place between the leaders of the US, China and Russia as “extremely significant” but pointed out that any agreements reached at the meeting cannot be imposed on other nations.

articles.title_orig: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
articles.title_zh: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
articles.content_orig:
Foundation Future Industries , a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.
The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak , borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.
Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.
A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts .
Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.
The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.
"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.
That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.
Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.
"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands."
Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.
"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."
Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."
While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.
Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.
Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.
In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors , claims the automaker rejected.
Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.
Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.
Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.
That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.
"This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"
Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.
Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.
The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.
Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon -owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.
Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury , Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.
Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their FDIC-backed accounts.
While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC chair Jelena McWilliams , said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.
The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.
Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.
Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, the Wall Street Journal reported last year. The WSJ report didn't mention Pathak specifically.
The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.
"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said . "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

articles.title_orig: A new 'Yalta'? Trump and Putin push for a meeting that Xi is wary of hosting
articles.title_zh: A new 'Yalta'? Trump and Putin push for a meeting that Xi is wary of hosting
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump will meet jointly next week with China’s leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the White House said Friday, a first-ever trilateral sit-down between the leaders of the three countries.
The meeting, on the sidelines of the APEC summit in China, will focus on nuclear non-proliferation, a topic Trump has said he believes could yield a new agreement between the world’s biggest nuclear-armed states.
“The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous,” Olivia Wales, a White House spokesman, told reporters.
The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia expired in February.
China, meanwhile, has been rapidly building its nuclear arsenal.
Officials downplayed the prospect of striking a new deal on nuclear matters, suggesting instead the talks would be a starting point.
“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior US official said. “I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level, between these countries.”
“So this is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward,” the official went on.
Officials said the world leaders also planned to discuss Iran.
A senior US official said Elon Musk is expected to go on the trip with Trump, among others, though he is not expected to attend the trilateral meeting.
Beijing and Moscow have yet to officially confirm participation in the trilateral summit.

articles.title_orig: US floats Nato membership for Donbas withdrawal deal, Zelenskyy says
articles.title_zh: US floats Nato membership for Donbas withdrawal deal, Zelenskyy says
articles.content_orig:
US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
The Ukrainian president's comments on Saturday come after US envoys visited Moscow and an EU summit in Dublin as part of ongoing efforts to end the war between Russia and Ukraine.
Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance to deter future threats, but this previously been opposed by the US and others while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.
Zelensky has also consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory, despite Moscow's demands for it to cede the Donbas.
"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky told reporters on Saturday.
He went on to say that if he received a proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.
US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow.
Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted, and that Moscow's demands for territory and neutrality continue to far exceed what Ukraine is prepared to consider.
Moscow has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.
Ukraine has rejected these, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.
There have, however, been recent signs the two can find common ground: last month, US First Lady Melania Trump was able to broker a temporary ceasefire in the the Kherson region to allow for evacuations and aid deliveries.
US officials had previously said that Ukrainian Nato membership was off the table.
Zelensky said on Saturday that the US proposal made him believe that "Nato is back on the agenda".
But he cautioned: "You have also heard Putin's signals, and this is an extremely difficult conversation."
Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.
Ceding the small portions of land Ukraine still controls there would be symbolically significant for Kyiv because it would constitute an acceptance of the Donbas being Russian.
Zelensky has previously spoken of retaking Russian-controlled territory in four of Ukraine's regions, as well as the Crimean peninsula, which Moscow annexed in 2014.
The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices, which have been rising since the US and Israel attacked Iran in February.
Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.
Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

articles.title_orig: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.title_zh: China holds 80% of underwater data center patents in past 20 years, can boost AI energy use
articles.content_orig:
China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents.
Two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026 reported this finding.
They also found that China holds the lion's share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
A new study has found that China owns around 80 percent of all global underwater data center patents. That’s not to say China owns much of the technology used in these setups, but it does reveal how active it has been in patenting in this field.
The study’s findings come from two Chinese researchers analyzing 168 patents filed between 2006 and 2026. It appears to show that technological focus has shifted quite dramatically over this time.
Before about 2014, patents were dominated by American, Norwegian, and Canadian researchers exploring underwater enclosures and pressure protection. Between about 2015 and 2020, attention turned to cooling, electrical supply, and long-term reliability.
From 2021, Chinese researchers became the dominant source for patents, particularly focusing on modular construction and maintenance. They also found that China holds the lion’s share, with South Korea owning around 17, and the rest split between the US and Europe.
Chinese patents in particular focus on the actual construction, installation, connections, and maintenance of them at scale. This appears to show that China is shifting focus to the more practical elements rather than proving experimental technology.
All very interesting, but why all the interest? Well, data centers generate an enormous amount of heat when in operation. This comes from the conversion of electricity into heat by the vast number of computer processors.
Typically, this is handled by using a combination of fans, chillers, cooling towers, and liquid-cooling systems to manage temperatures. That is costly in terms of hardware and additional electricity costs.
If the centers could be placed underwater, they could take advantage of the ocean’s near-limitless supply of very cold seawater. Obviously, you can’t just submerge the hardware directly into the ocean, so they need to be placed inside sealed, pressure-resistant containers first.
These are then lowered and secured to the seabed, and connections are made to the shore for power and data cables. Once there, the heat from the servers can be transferred to the cold ocean water using special internal cooling systems.
To this end, the seawater acts as a massive heat sink, potentially eliminating much of the mechanical cooling equipment needed on land. This doesn’t make the computers themselves consume less electricity, but it can reduce the energy spent keeping them cool.
And it is not just a theoretical technology either. Famously, Microsoft deployed one, called Project Natick , off the coast of Scotland in 2018. The project ran for around two years, and results were very encouraging.
According to Microsoft, the underwater data center had just one-eighth of the failure rate of similar land-based setups. Yet despite this, Microsoft chose not to commercialize the technology, and confirmed in 2024 that the project had been discontinued.
So, is the 80 percent figure something other nations should sit up and take notice of? Yes, and no. It is clear China has established some kind of lead here in terms of patents, but the engineering challenges of actually deploying them are enormous.
The shift in focus to modularity likely reflects China’s ambitions to scale the technology commercially. But it is important to note that patents tend to be territorial in nature.
Holding a large share of patents in a particular field doesn’t automatically give a country control of the technology worldwide.
Christopher graduated from Cardiff University in 2004 with a Masters Degree in Geology. Since then, he has worked exclusively within the Built Environment, Occupational Health and Safety and Environmental Consultancy industries. He is a qualified and accredited Energy Consultant, Green Deal Assessor and Practitioner member of IEMA. Chris’s main interests range from Science and Engineering, Military and Ancient History to Politics and Philosophy.

articles.title_orig: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.title_zh: The Surprise Censorship Battle Over My Cocktail Book Has Left Me Shaken—and Stirred
articles.content_orig:
DEAR ABBY : My sister-in-law “Leah” has been a poor money manager all her life. She is in significant credit card debt and had to borrow money to help pay for her wedding, despite the fact that she has been a teacher for decades. She has never been a saver — always a spender.
When my husband passed away recently, he left me with $1 million in life insurance proceeds. When Leah found out about it (I’m not sure how), she asked me to lend her some money to get back on her feet. When I refused, my other sister-in-law chastised me, saying that my husband would have lent her the money. Leah has been bailed out a few times by her sister but never by my husband. Am I wrong to stand my ground? — NOT AN ENABLER
DEAR NOT AN ENABLER : My heart goes out to you for the loss of your husband. Leah may be using the word “lend,” but believe me when I say you would never see that money again. If she wants to get out of debt, she needs to speak to a credit counselor, not her brother’s grieving widow. If she brings it up again, tell her to visit the National Foundation for Credit Counseling at nfcc.org.
DEAR ABBY : I am a 70-year-old divorced man. For the past 10 years, my ex-wife has been living with me. Due to her medical condition and lack of family support, she has no one else to assist her. My own health is declining, so caring for her is a physical strain and emotionally stressful. She refuses any suggestion of a senior living facility because her only income is a small Social Security benefit.
How do I move on without fighting and accusations? I know I facilitated this by allowing her into my home in the first place. Any ideas where to begin? — FRUSTRATED IN TEXAS
DEAR FRUSTRATED : You were kind to take in and care for your ex a decade ago, but this arrangement is now affecting your health. To protect your own well-being, you must put your foot down. Help your ex-wife one last time by finding her a facility she can afford. Do not expect the transition to be pleasant, but the result will be an improvement for both of you.
DEAR ABBY : I am a happily married woman who went through a midlife crisis more than 20 years ago. At the time, I left my husband for another man, who gave me an expensive cocktail ring. When my relationship with the new man started to suffer for various reasons, I returned to my husband. Our marriage has remained strong ever since.
I have never worn the ring and have always felt guilty for having it. Should I contact my former lover and return it? Should I pawn it and send him the proceeds? Or maybe you have another suggestion? — RINGS HOLLOW IN ARIZONA
DEAR RINGS HOLLOW : Sell the ring and donate the proceeds to a worthy charitable cause. Do not open the door to further contact with your former lover.
Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at http://www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.

articles.title_orig: In Jensen Huang’s Ouster, Tech Billionaires See a Mistake—and a Lesson
articles.title_zh: In Jensen Huang’s Ouster, Tech Billionaires See a Mistake—and a Lesson
articles.content_orig:
Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.
But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.
Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.
She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.
The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.
The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

The meeting point had been arranged: near 81st Street and Broadway on the Upper West Side.
It was there, in broad daylight, that two men approached each other on a Wednesday in April 2025. One of the men, a 67-year-old New Yorker, transported a bag of $9 million in gold bars, each one the size of a chocolate bar, that the police said someone online had instructed him to buy and hand over.
The man did exactly as he was told, believing that he could secure his financial assets, which an alert on his computer had led to believe were compromised, the authorities said.
The other man took sack of gold and fled on foot, according to the police. The first man had been the victim of an online fraud.
Now, more than a year and a half after the deceit, the New York Police Department is asking for the public’s help in identifying the man who ran off with the gold bars in connection with a grand larceny investigation.
Investigators this week released security camera footage and images of the man suspected of taking the bars.
Isaac Kahan, the owner of Bullion Trading LLC , a gold and silver dealer in Manhattan’s Diamond District, wondered about the sheer logistics that were involved in the heist.
