articles.title_orig: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores pricing essentials 30% below retail
articles.title_zh: NYC is spending $70 million on 5 city-run grocery stores pricing essentials 30% below retail
articles.content_orig:
New York City is moving closer to launching its effort to counter food inflation by opening five city-run grocery stores. Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced in May 2026 that the first store would open in the Hunts Point neighborhood of the South Bronx in 2027, with another in East Harlem to follow.
Five stores, one in each borough, are unlikely to substantially change grocery prices in a city with nearly 1,000 supermarkets and more than 8 million inhabitants . But each could make a meaningful difference to the grocery bills of local shoppers by selling essentials at below-market prices.
Even with just five planned stores set to open in lower-income neighborhoods, the initiative has ignited fierce opposition from independent grocers , supermarket trade associations and a coalition representing immigrant-owned food businesses .
What explains this pushback?
As a food policy scholar , I believe this opposition is about more than the immediate economic impact of five stores. It is about the precedent they could establish. Mamdani’s initiative challenges an entrenched expectation that the government should leave the provision of consumer goods to private enterprise even as it encourages businesses to invest in certain locations, regulates their activities and helps low-income shoppers through various food assistance programs.
The reality is more complicated. For at least a century, New York’s food economy has not operated independently of government . In fact, public policies and investments have long shaped where supermarkets open, which businesses can operate with a profit, and how residents obtain food.
It’s just that they have done so in ways consumers often don’t see.
That is why the five grocery stores carry a broader significance, in my view. They offer a different model of public investment that makes the government much more visible in providing an essential service – and more accountable for its results. New Yorkers will get an opportunity to judge that contribution directly.
If the stores succeed, they may change not just what people expect to pay for groceries, but what they expect their city government to provide.
New York City has committed US$70 million to develop these stores, which will be open to all.
While they will be managed by private operators, the city will provide rent-free space, prioritize publicly owned sites and ensure that essential foods are priced 30% below typical retail prices.
In this respect, the stores offer a “ public option ” – a government-provided good or service that exists alongside private alternatives , like public schools and city hospitals.
Municipal grocery stores would offer New Yorkers a similar choice alongside private retailers. But as a public option, they would create a visible alternative against which shoppers can judge privately owned stores, setting a benchmark for food prices and service quality. They would also demonstrate how public investment can be used to make an essential good more affordable.
At his May announcement , Mamdani described the proposed Bronx store and its surrounding development as “physical proof of our conviction that government can be a force for good.”
Government-supported food retailing has a long history in New York City despite opposition by existing businesses.
In 1934, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia’s administration began selling discounted milk to low-income families, but the initiative drew complaints from grocers about unfair competition. Independent merchants similarly protested the city’s efforts to subsidize a new Pathmark supermarket in East Harlem in the 1990s, warning that it would put local grocers out of business.
A more recent example is the city’s Food Retail Expansion to Support Health program , known as FRESH. Since 2009, it has offered supermarket developers and operators long-term tax breaks and zoning incentives to build or expand dozens of stores in underserved neighborhoods.
These incentives have helped increase grocery retail space, but shoppers don’t see the public support behind them.
FRESH is just one example of an approach toward supermarket financing that gained momentum in the 1990s, when governments sought to address social problems by encouraging private investment. Food insecurity was blamed on a scarcity of neighborhood supermarkets, not on prices being beyond reach for local shoppers.
Subsidizing new stores promised better nutrition and economic development without confronting poverty or inequality, and FRESH reflects that approach. Participating supermarkets must devote space to perishable foods, but they’re not required to offer affordable prices. That may be one reason why researchers have found that adding supermarkets to low-income neighborhoods, by itself, doesn’t substantially improve residents’ diets.
This hidden government role is hardly confined to grocery stores. Much of what government does for Americans is delivered indirectly, through tax credits, subsidies and private institutions. Because the public contribution is obscured, people often give credit to private markets for the benefits provided by public policy, from student loans to healthcare.
This invisibility is a consequence of policy design and influences how citizens understand government, a phenomenon that political scientist Suzanne Mettler described as “ the submerged state .”
Municipal grocery stores depart from the traditional model in two important ways.
First, they make affordability an explicit condition of public investment rather than the outcome of increased retail competition. Second, they make government’s contribution visible. For example, the stores will share distinct branding so shoppers know who’s responsible for the affordable food.
If the stores deliver reliable savings, shoppers may begin to see affordable food as something government can help provide, not an outcome determined entirely by private markets. When public benefits are obscured, people are more likely to underestimate government’s contribution to their lives. Visible programs, like a physical store in the neighborhood, make that contribution easier to notice and evaluate.
Visibility also creates accountability. A customer at a private supermarket that received a tax break to expand isn’t likely to tie the store’s prices or food quality to government policy. At a municipal grocery store, with clear branding, the connection is unmistakable.
To be sure, critics’ concerns deserve serious attention. Many independent grocery stores are owned by immigrant entrepreneurs operating on thin margins. Groups representing bodegas and independent supermarkets warn that a publicly subsidized competitor could draw away their customers. Some may lose business.
Yet East Harlem’s Pathmark demonstrates that new supermarkets and smaller retailers can coexist. Between 2000 and 2015, the number of small grocery stores and bodegas in the neighborhood increased from 100 to 126 , while supermarkets rose from 10 to 18. That said, those figures don’t establish Pathmark’s effects on individual businesses.
The municipal stores’ impact on nearby retailers remains an open question. But the task for New York City is to ensure that private operators deliver excellent service and real savings, and that their commercial interests don’t undermine the public mission. It will also need to provide good working conditions and track effects on nearby businesses.
Ultimately, public ownership doesn’t guarantee success. But it makes government’s responsibility for the outcome impossible to miss.
Nevin Cohen , Chair of the Department of Health Policy and Management, CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Public Policy

articles.title_orig: Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks
articles.title_zh: Finland rejects reported Russian demand to leave NATO as part of peace talks
articles.content_orig:
Finland has rejected a reported Russian demand that it leave NATO as part of Ukraine peace talks, with Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen saying its membership in the alliance wasn’t up for negotiation.
"Such matters are in no way a matter for negotiation. Russia knows that. This is absolutely outrageous to even suggest such a thing," Häkkänen told reporters on Friday , according to Finnish broadcaster Yle. Finland, which shares a 1,340-kilometer border with Russia, joined NATO in 2023 in a foreign policy U-turn prompted by the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
German newspaper Bild reported that a Russian proposal made during talks in Abu Dhabi this week included Moscow keeping occupied Ukrainian territories, gaining control of new swathes of land, demilitarizing ports in Ukraine, removing NATO bases from the Baltics, and Finland leaving NATO.
Russia proposed withdrawing its nuclear weapons from Belarus and refraining from stationing intermediate-range missiles there in exchange, Bild reported.
But it remains unclear which proposals Russian President Vladimir Putin would support after discussions between intermediaries, according to the report.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a new security framework for Europe for after the war raised by the Americans “can be dangerous."
“Russia certainly cannot make decisions on behalf of all the societies that are members of NATO,” he told reporters on Friday.
Zelenskyy’s comments were not in direct response to the demands reported by Bild, but came after a meeting between Zelenskyy and U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner on Thursday in Dublin .
“Putin's desire to change borders in Europe is a fact. I am sure this is part of his concept of revising security guarantees in Europe. This is dangerous because, in my view, it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title_orig: Jensen Huang's $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get
articles.title_zh: Jensen Huang's $145 billion question: What California divorce law says Lori Huang could get
articles.content_orig:
Jensen Huang has lost his job, his board seat, and roughly $10 billion in paper wealth since admitting to an affair. If his 41-year marriage ends, California law could put a far larger share of his fortune in play.
Huang stepped down as Nvidia’s president, CEO, and director this week, days after confessing in a letter to Nvidia employees that he had been unfaithful to Lori Huang, his wife since 1985. The board named chief financial officer Colette Kress Nvidia’s interim CEO and made longtime director Harvey Jones its first board chair while it searches for a permanent successor.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang wrote.
“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
The admission followed a New York Times report that U.S. intelligence agencies suspected Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data center company Megaspeed, of gathering information for Beijing, and that she had a close relationship with Huang. China has denied involvement. Singapore’s Ministry of Home Affairs said this week that she left Singapore in February and was barred from returning after a police investigation, which it said “did not concern espionage.”
Two more relationships have since been reported. The New York Times reported on November 11 that Huang had been romantically involved with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, who reported directly to him, citing five people who had worked at the company. A day later, Reuters reported that Huang had an intimate relationship with another Nvidia employee , whom it did not name. Powell did not respond to the Times, and Nvidia declined to comment to Reuters .
Nvidia’s board opened an independent investigation into whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort and said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.” An FBI inquiry into his relationship with Alice Huang is also underway.
Huang has not announced plans to divorce. But a split would test how California divides a fortune built almost entirely on a single stock, and the answer would turn less on his headline net worth than on how the couple’s Nvidia shares were acquired and held.
Huang reported beneficial ownership of about 870.6 million Nvidia shares, or 3.58% of the company’s outstanding stock, as of March 23, 2026, according to Nvidia’s 2026 proxy statement . Nvidia ranked No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500 and was the first company on the list worth more than $4 trillion .
Jensen and Lori Huang are co-trustees of their living trust, which holds about 528.5 million shares, and of two other family trusts. Together, the three trusts hold nearly 669 million shares. Another 73.3 million shares are held by limited liability companies whose sole member is the living trust.
Lori Huang also runs the family’s philanthropy. She is president of the Jen-Hsun & Lori Huang Foundation, which reported about $9.2 billion in assets at the end of 2024, Fortune reported . The foundation holds about 58.7 million Nvidia shares, but the proxy states that neither spouse has a pecuniary interest in them.
The distinction matters. Beneficial ownership and control of shares do not by themselves establish personal ownership, or determine how assets would be divided in a divorce.
The couple met as lab partners at Oregon State University and married in 1985, eight years before Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993. They live in California, a community-property state, where assets acquired during a marriage are generally owned jointly and divided equally in a divorce.
“In California, all property acquired by a spouse during marriage is community property,” Christopher Melcher, a Los Angeles attorney who specializes in high-net-worth divorces, told the New York Post . “She would be entitled to 50%.”
Under California Courts guidance , community property generally includes earnings and assets acquired between the date of marriage and the date of separation. Property owned before the marriage or acquired after separation, along with gifts and inheritances, is generally separate property, and some assets can be a mix of both.
That means Lori Huang could be entitled to half of the community-property portion of the couple’s Nvidia holdings, not necessarily half of every share tied to her husband.
The outcome would depend on how the shares were acquired, how the trusts are structured, whether separate and community assets were mixed, and whether the couple signed a prenuptial or postnuptial agreement. A court would need to examine those details before deciding what either spouse receives.
California is also a no-fault divorce state , meaning either spouse can seek a divorce without proving infidelity or other wrongdoing. Infidelity, even across several reported relationships, generally does not entitle one spouse to a larger share of community property.
Huang is worth about $145 billion and ranks as the world’s 13th-richest person, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index, as Fortune reported . That figure is a market estimate, not a tally of marital property, and it rises and falls with Nvidia’s stock, which shed $450 billion in market value in the days after his admission.
Huang has described his wife’s role in the company in plain terms. “Every moment of Nvidia, she was there,” he said in an interview with CNA.

articles.title_orig: Nearly $20m found in Hungary’s forests, buildings amid corruption probe
articles.title_zh: Nearly $20m found in Hungary’s forests, buildings amid corruption probe
articles.content_orig:
Hungary seizes $18m cash tied to ex-Orban-era minister in probe
Hungarian investigators have found $19.5m in hidden cash, including bundles dug out in forests, during a corruption probe involving a former minister under ex-Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office, a new agency set up to investigate suspected misuse of public money, said in a statement late on Friday that searches took place on November 12 and 13 in Budapest and three other parts of Hungary.
Its investigators found Hungarian forints, euros and US dollars in farm buildings, warehouses, a home and “a high-value safe in a secluded location”, as well as beneath the ground in forests. The agency released footage showing officers digging outdoors after dark and examining piles of cash, which was later deposited with the state treasury.
Finance Minister Andras Karman said on Facebook on Friday that 12 treasury employees spent eight hours counting it.
The discovery comes amid an investigation into Miklos Sesztak, Hungary’s development minister from 2014 to 2018, who is suspected of receiving more than $37.2m in bribes and kickbacks tied to overpriced secondhand bus purchases by a state transport company and government construction projects.
He was detained in September and denies wrongdoing.
Prime Minister Peter Magyar, whose centre-right, pro-European Tisza party ended Orban’s 16 years in power in April, said on Facebook on Friday that the recovery signalled the end of what he called the “Fidesz-KDNP mafia”.
Fidesz is Orban’s right-wing party, while KDNP, the Christian Democratic People’s Party, was its smaller governing ally.
Orban has previously accused the new government of using the investigations to force him out of politics.
Other former ministers have been arrested in separate cases, as has Gyorgy Matolcsy, the former governor of Hungary’s central bank, which sets monetary policy.
His case concerns alleged misuse of public assets held by a central bank foundation. Matolcsy has denied wrongdoing.
A survey published this week by Hungarian news website HVG by pollster Median suggested that 70 percent of respondents considered investigating suspected corruption under Orban and holding those responsible accountable very important.

articles.title_orig: Prediction: Nov. 18 Will Be a Massive Day for the Stock Market
articles.title_zh: Prediction: Nov. 18 Will Be a Massive Day for the Stock Market
articles.content_orig:
Artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, heavily weighted in the S&P 500 , have fueled its direction in recent years. In the early stages of the AI boom, the direction was clearly upward, but in 2026, the major index has delivered a mix of gains and declines. And the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite even entered correction territory earlier this month.
Though companies in the AI space continue to report significant growth and speak of strong demand, investors have become cautious. Investors are more focused today on headwinds such as rising inflation and risks such as the possibility that the AI revenue opportunity will fall short of expectations. And this is against the backdrop of tremendous spending on AI infrastructure, with tech giants pouring more than $700 billion into the build-out this year.
Considering AI's spot center stage, I predict that Nov. 18 will be a massive day for the stock market. For two reasons. Let's zoom in for a close look.
Image source: Getty Images.
First, though, it's important to talk a bit more about what's happened so far. The S&P 500 has soared over the past three calendar years and extended the gain into 2026 on optimism about the potential of AI. The technology is already resulting in explosive earnings growth for companies developing it, but it is also on track to boost the earnings of companies that apply it to their needs. AI has what it takes to make companies more efficient and innovative. As a result, AI could significantly reshape the corporate earnings picture down the road.
Investors jumped to get in on this space, buying shares of AI chip designers like Nvidia and cloud service providers like Alphabet . These stocks and other tech giants, heavily weighted in the S&P 500, set the mood for the entire market. And it was generally positive for quite some time.
This year, however, a more difficult economic backdrop, with higher inflation, has weighed on investors' appetite for growth-oriented companies. Higher prices and potential interest rate hikes aimed at controlling inflation both represent headwinds for these players. Meanwhile, investors have questioned whether companies spending big on AI chips and data centers will be able to successfully monetize the infrastructure.
All of this has made investors particularly attentive to messages from and the actions of leading players in the AI space. And this brings me to my prediction. Nov. 18 may be huge for the stock market because of two events.
First, on Nov. 17, after the market closes, AI chip leader Nvidia is scheduled to report third-quarter earnings. The company has reported quarter after quarter of growth and record revenue levels and spoken of ongoing strong demand. Nvidia forecasts revenue of $108 billion for the period and gross margins of 74%. We also may be on the lookout for comments on the rollout of Nvidia's latest platform, Vera Rubin, and first-ever stand-alone central processing units (CPUs). These chips could unlock a $200 billion revenue opportunity for the company.
Nvidia's comments may offer the stock market direction during the following trading session, on Nov. 18, as the company is the key player in the AI story. Excitement about the Anthropic initial public offering may also drive the market on this day. CNBC, citing people familiar with the situation, reports that Anthropic will price on Nov. 18 and begin trading on Nov. 19.
The AI lab, which may enter the market with a trillion-dollar valuation, will offer investors a fresh AI bet. Anthropic, the developer of the famous model Claude, has seen its revenue soar more than 1,200% year over year in the first nine months of this year to about $33 billion. This IPO could provide overall market momentum in the latter part of the week.

articles.title_orig: Regular coffee drinking linked to changes in gut motility and microbiome
articles.title_zh: Regular coffee drinking linked to changes in gut motility and microbiome
articles.content_orig:
A scientific study carried out by the University of Copenhagen has found that drinking coffee regularly may affect the functioning of the digestive system, especially bowel movements and colon contractions and is also linked to greater diversity of gut bacteria.
The study was published in the journal "Gut Microbiology", which specialises in research on gut microorganisms, and aimed to explore the relationship between habitual coffee consumption and the physiological conditions inside the digestive system.
The research team used a small electronic capsule that participants swallowed to track the changes that occurred as it travelled through the digestive system.
The capsule measured a set of indicators, including the time it took contents to pass through the gastrointestinal tract, temperature, acidity levels and intestinal contractions.
The study involved 61 healthy adults in Denmark, whom the researchers divided into two groups according to how much coffee they consumed.
The first group consisted of people who drank between one and five cups of coffee a day on more than three of the eight days covered by the study, while the second group comprised people who drank coffee less frequently.
The results showed that people who consume coffee regularly have greater diversity in the microorganisms present in their intestines compared with participants who drink less coffee.
This finding is consistent with research suggesting that coffee may influence the composition of the gut microbiome, the community of bacteria and other microorganisms that live inside the digestive system.
Francesca Bucci, the lead researcher in the study and a PhD student in the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, said that regular coffee consumption seems to affect the physiology of the intestines.
One of the most notable results was that people who drink coffee regularly had much lower acidity levels in the small intestine than those who consume it less often.
The researchers also observed a link between higher coffee intake and a greater number of contractions in the colon, muscle movements that help push intestinal contents through the digestive system.
These contractions play a role in digestion and in keeping bowel movements regular, as they help move waste along and may help prevent constipation and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition.
Bucci said that intestinal contractions can support proper digestion, help reduce constipation and help maintain the functional state of the intestinal muscles.
By contrast, the researchers are still unable to determine whether the lower level of acidity in the small intestine benefits health or could have negative effects.
The researchers stress that the study cannot prove that coffee consumption is the direct cause of the changes observed in the digestive system.
However, Henrik Munch Roager, associate professor and head of the research group in the Department of Nutrition, Exercise and Sports at the University of Copenhagen, believes there are reasons to support the possibility that coffee plays a role in these changes.
He explained that previous studies have shown that coffee affects a range of processes that take place inside the digestive system, including the secretion of acids in the stomach.
He added that this evidence makes it likely that the differences the researchers observed are linked to the effects of coffee rather than being mere coincidence.
He pointed out that many people notice, based on their daily experience, that coffee affects their digestion.
The research team sees the next step as conducting a study that allows control over the amount of coffee participants drink, instead of merely observing their consumption habits and comparing the differences between them.
This type of study would help determine whether coffee is actually causing these changes and to understand the mechanisms through which it may affect bowel movements and contractions.

articles.title_orig: Trump to hold trilateral talks with Xi, Putin in China next week: White House
articles.title_zh: Trump to hold trilateral talks with Xi, Putin in China next week: White House
articles.content_orig:
US President Donald Trump will meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in China next week for trilateral talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit, the White House said Friday.
The meeting will take place in Shenzhen.
"The President has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," Assistant Press Secretary Olivia Wales told reporters on a call.
Trump will also hold a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi on Thursday afternoon before concluding his visit to China with the trilateral meeting, Wales said.
A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said Washington does not expect an agreement to emerge from the talks.
"I would characterize this as the entry point, the first conversation, certainly at the leader level between these countries," the official said.
The official said China's nuclear arsenal is "growing by far the fastest in the world" and argued that it was time for Beijing to "step up to the adult table."
Trump plans to discuss Iran in the trilateral meeting but not Ukraine, the official said, because China is not part of the separate US-Russia track.

I t’s beginning to look a lot like 2017, thanks to ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
The Nvidia co-founder’s career has spontaneously combusted since he admitted last week to an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman who U.S. officials suspect of being an asset or agent of China’s Ministry of State Security, its equivalent of the CIA.
A trio of House committee chairs have demanded Huang appear before Congress to brief them on his ties to Ms. Huang (no relation).
On Monday, The New York Times revealed that he’d also had a second affair with one of his subordinates, leading Nvidia’s board to move towards tossing him out of the company he’d started three decades earlier.
The tech billionaire’s problems have brought about a temporal vibe shift — reviving and exposing Trump administration infighting and leaking at a level not seen since the heady early months of the president’s chaotic first White House term.
To start, the Times scooped that Marco Rubio, Secretary of State cum National Security Adviser, was so sufficiently alarmed at what U.S. intelligence officials were learning about Alice Huang through electronic surveillance that he drafted a classified memorandum detailing how she’d allegedly been recruited by the Chinese spy agency.
The goal of the Chinese operation was reportedly to send Alice Huang to target Jensen Huang in hopes of learning more about his products and influencing him to push Nvidia towards selling Beijing more of the company’s cutting-edge AI chips, according to reports.
Rubio was so concerned by what he read about the Nvidia CEO’s relationship with Alice Huang that he made a point of briefing President Donald Trump on the memorandum while aboard Air Force One en route to China this past May.
Yet the Secretary of State’s warnings appeared to have little effect on Trump. He was so hell-bent on having Huang travel with him to Beijing that he ordered his Air Force One crew to wait at an Alaska air base for Huang to meet him there on a private jet.
Trump appeared to have been taken in by a charm offensive the then-Nvidia CEO was mounting to convince him to relax export controls on his company’s top-end chips.
The Biden administration had restricted their export out of concern that acquiring them could help foreign adversaries (mainly Beijing) gain an advantage over the U.S. in the race to develop the most advanced AI models.
Huang’s effort was incredibly successful.
Having curried favor with the president by way of a $25 million corporate donation to the controversial White House ballroom project, Trump and his allies began giving Huang a freer hand in who he sold his products to. In turn, Huang became a frequent visitor to the White House.
At the same time, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — the U.S. official responsible for administering the country’s export control regime — was reportedly refusing to impose any sanctions on Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, despite serious concerns from the U.S. intelligence community over whether the company was serving as a front for Beijing’s efforts to acquire more of Nvidia’s top-end products.
Now, with Huang having been forcibly exited from the empire he built, the scrutiny is intensifying on Lutnick.
Administration officials have always been reluctant to so much as hint at criticizing Trump, and his cozy relationship and seeming willful ignorance of Jensen Huang’s dalliance with an alleged Chinese honeypot is no exception.
But the Commerce Secretary, a longtime friend of Trump’s going back to their days as New York City high-rollers, does not inspire the same fear.
Newly resurfaced audio, from the tech bro favorite All In podcast, reveals him boasting about his own close relationship with Huang, who he called a “national treasure” that he had brought into Trump’s inner circle.
“I promised him in the beginning when I first met him that I would help him have really easy access to the president,” Lutnick said during a podcast taping in January, speaking to a cohort of hosts that included the then-White House AI Czar, David Sacks.
He described how Huang sold Trump on relaxing export controls by arguing that it would keep China dependent on his own AI chips rather than building up domestic manufacturing, and said Trump agreed with the caveat that Nvidia pay a 25 percent tariff when importing them into the U.S. for testing.
“He (Huang) has to send the chips to America. We test the chip to make sure that he hasn’t enhanced it in any way... On the way in, we can charge it a tariff, a regular 25 percent tariff, and then we can give export licenses to whoever he wants to sell it to. He sends it to China, or he sends it to whoever he’s selling it to,” Lutnick said.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent wasted no time pointing the finger Friday when he told CNBC that it was the Lutnick-led Commerce Department who resisted putting Megaspeed, the China-linked company, on his department’s “Entity List” of companies not allowed to purchase American products.
Asked whether the Trump administration considered adding Megaspeed to the list, Bessent replied: “I can tell you there was coordination. It was Treasury, War, [the U.S. trade representative], and State. They were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months. But Commerce has the pen.”
Then, he twisted the knife.
“You will have to ask them about their internal process,” he said.
More embarrassment for Lutnick came in the form of a leak to Axios revealing that he’d been one of the officials who’d received the Rubio memorandum warning about Jensen Huang’s ties to Alice Huang and Megaspeed.
And things may get worse. Lutnick is scheduled to testify before Congress on this very matter within days.
Last time he was on Capitol Hill, he gave a questionable performance under questioning about his relationship with deceased sex abuser Jeffrey Epstein.
This time, he will have to explain why he didn’t care that one of America’s most important companies was selling sensitive products to a company with suspected links to Chinese espionage.

articles.title_orig: Huge crowds and low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as Pope Leo XIV visits South America
articles.title_zh: Huge crowds and low vaccination rates raise measles alarms as Pope Leo XIV visits South America
articles.content_orig:
Prison chaplain Father Matías de Martini said the pontiff’s visit to the prison reminds us that God “rejoices over the sheep that has been found, the son who returns home.”
Father Matías de Martini, chaplain of the Devoto prison in Buenos Aires, Argentina, could not hold back his tears as he thanked Pope Leo XIV for his visit to the penitentiary on Nov. 11 and for his genuine concern for the inmates.
The priest said the pontiff’s visit “reminds us once again that God does not consider anyone lost, that he rejoices over the lost sheep, the son who returns home.”
On Nov. 11, Pope Leo XIV brought a message full of hope to the prisoners.
Addressing them, their families, and prison staff, he reflected on the “experience of our limitations” that human beings encounter. “Often,” he noted, “we become aware of our limitations through sin and its consequences, whether by making a mistake, suffering from an illness, or experiencing the death of a loved one.”
However, he said that, “even amid the evil, pain, and deepest failures you may have experienced or caused, your present circumstances can become an opportunity to begin your lives anew, as you have shared with us in your testimonies.”
The pope emphasized that “human beings do not flourish in spite of their limitations, but often through them,” and pointed out that “prison is also a witness to profound changes and conversions, to growth, learning, and the acquisition of new skills and knowledge.”
For this reason, he assured the prisoners that “with God’s grace, it is possible to move beyond total darkness and kindle small lights of hope.”
At the conclusion of his address, he turned to the families and encouraged them to look to Jesus, who was himself a prisoner, and to pray that he might “grant them all strength and wisdom, so that this time of solitude and isolation will not be in vain, but will become a time of grace and salvation.”
“We are part of the same human family. Let us promote whatever contributes to the good of all. Let us accompany especially our children and young people, educating them in authentic values, caring for them and protecting them, so that they do not fall into the pernicious networks of criminality,” the pope said.
De Martini thanked the pontiff, saying that “through your presence we feel the embrace of the Father, an embrace that makes no distinction based on the past, an embrace that reminds us of our dignity, something that nothing and no one can take away.”
The priest also recalled that “we are beloved children, and it is this truth — the deepest truth — that makes us completely free.”
Cristian, 29, is an inmate who shared his testimony with the Holy Father. The young prisoner recounted the details of a past marked by drug and alcohol use which drove him to commit crimes to sustain his addiction.
“All of that ended up distancing me from my family and the people who love me. I lost my job; I lost everything,” he lamented. However, he continued, “Jesus transformed my life during the time I was living on the streets.”
The young man recounted with hope how he encountered Jesus after going to the prison chapel.
“There, I felt that I was not alone, that Jesus was with me, calling me to reencounter him. I decided to follow him, convinced that he is the true path. I felt him touch my heart. I allowed myself to be guided, and he removed the blindfold from my eyes. I was able to see reality, and that truth is what makes me free on the inside today. From that moment on, everything began to make sense,” he noted.
Cristian, an inmate, shares his testimony at Devoto Prison in Buenos Aires. | Credit: Daniel Ibáñez/EWTN News
His time in prison is “transforming my life,” said 32-year-old Maximiliano, who also shared his testimony with the Holy Father.
He recalled how drugs and alcohol had distanced him from his family, especially his daughters. He said that while in prison, he found inner freedom through an encounter with Jesus.
Reinaldo embraces Pope Leo XIV. | Credit: Daniel Ibáñez/EWTN News
Reinaldo, 44, recently completed his prison sentence and was able to reunite with his family and his four children.
He said prison was the setting “where Jesus, Our Lord and friend, offered me a new opportunity, a new life.”
Reinaldo described placing his faith in Jesus as “an embrace” that heals the soul. “Today, as each new day begins, I keep in mind what it was like to return to the arms of Jesus — that sincere embrace, that embrace of forgiveness, that embrace of a Father who loves his son; an embrace that instilled in me a new hope and a profound certainty of knowing that I am a beloved son.”
This story was first published by EWTN News Español, the Spanish-language sister service of EWTN News. It has been translated and adapted by EWTN News English.

articles.title_orig: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
articles.title_zh: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
articles.content_orig:
Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.
“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.
But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.
“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”
This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one that is at the heart of mass antigovernment demonstrations planned for Saturday in France, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?
“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.

articles.title_orig: China Spy Claims Expose Global Tech Espionage
articles.title_zh: China Spy Claims Expose Global Tech Espionage
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's now ex-CEO left the post after it emerged he was romantically involved with a woman alleged to be spying for China, jolting the U.S. AI surge and thrusting allegations of Chinese penetration at major Western tech firms into the spotlight .
Beijing rejected the claims as a smear and said Washington is inventing "Chinese spy narratives" to rationalize curbs on technology exports. Even so, the operative suspected of involvement in the episode that precipitated Huang 's exit is currently in China and the Chinese government is aware of her presence.
What hangs in the balance is economic and military clout. The U.S. is betting a lead in AI and advanced chips will sustain its strength and help deter China over Taiwan, while espionage offers Beijing a way to narrow that lead and glean insight into U.S. military plans and political decision-making.
German prosecutors report that a married pair posed as interpreters and auto-sector workers to court academics across AI, computer science and aerospace, flying some to China to give paid "civilian" talks for state-owned defense companies.
According to New Zealand intelligence, a Chinese observatory closely linked to the government attempted to set up space-tracking gear via a domestic firm, equipment that might double as a tool for gathering military intelligence. Taiwan says Chinese agents trawl social media to find soldiers in debt, extend loans, and then demand sensitive information and referrals to fellow service members.
The Philippines offers a closer look at scale and sophistication. Authorities say suspected Chinese operatives claimed they flew drones loaded with fishing bait while observing warships near Subic Bay, and that another group pretended to be seafood purchasers as they piloted drones close to a naval installation. In Manila, contracted drivers equipped their cars with sham cellphone towers and cruised by the presidential palace, military encampments and the U.S. Embassy to scoop up nearby phone data.
A separate car outfitted with cameras plus mapping gear made stops at more than 120 sites, among them bases used by American forces. Officials add that presumed operatives cultivated sources within the defense establishment to secure rosters of naval personnel, timetables for troop rotations and resupply, and details on missions to outposts in the disputed South China Sea.
An investigator told Bloomberg the network encompassed hundreds. China has rejected the allegations as baseless.

Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro said the activity is widespread and not confined to the Philippines, pointing to cases in the United States, Australia and the United Kingdom.
Security agencies are turning up the volume. According to the Federal Bureau of Investigation, Chinese espionage is "a grave threat to the economic well-being" of the U.S. Britain's MI5 reported that in 2022 it was handling seven times the number of China-related probes as it had four years before. Canadian intelligence describes China as its "greatest counter-intelligence threat," while Dutch intelligence reports that Chinese digital espionage targeting technology firms is occurring on a "large scale."
China's Ministry of State Security is central to this push, combining overseas and domestic roles and, under Xi Jinping, tightening control over local bureaus to coordinate nationwide and pursue more ambitious missions abroad. Under the 2017 National Intelligence Law, every organization and citizen must "support, assist, and cooperate" with intelligence work.
Holden Triplett, who once led the FBI's Beijing office, said Chinese services have become highly professional, increasingly exploit human vulnerabilities, and that anyone can be susceptible.
With the AI revolution in full swing, Western officials say Chinese spy agencies have prioritized the technology that underpins it, seeking it through hacking and human sources.
AI is also changing tradecraft. "Human espionage doesn't anymore have to be sneaking around back alleys."
AI is also boosting cyber operations.
The bottom line: Washington is counting on AI and advanced chips to preserve economic and military heft, and the alleged espionage drive aims at those very advantages.

articles.title_orig: Some physical GTA 6 boxes are missing codes, with Rockstar refusing to help
articles.title_zh: Some physical GTA 6 boxes are missing codes, with Rockstar refusing to help
articles.content_orig:
Rockstar angered critics by opting against a physical disc for its latest title. Now, some pre-order holders are realizing that sealed cases also contain no digital code . As the GTA 6 release date looms, these customers are pleading with Rockstar and retailers for a solution.
Once fans collected their purchases, reports of missing redemptions in boxes mounted. While it doesn’t seem widespread, the issue is affecting both Xbox and PlayStation console owners. Social media accounts highlight one GTA 6 PS5 buyer showing how the inner sleeve displayed a gray strip instead of a code. Frustratingly, Best Buy refused to process a refund.
Even gamers who pre-ordered the GTA 6 physical version directly from Rockstar are facing the same predicament. Redditor InParties found the double-sided poster bonus waiting, but no PlayStation Store redemption. When asked for assistance, the studio closed two tickets.
The Rockstar website instructs customers who reserved copies from third-party retailers to contact those stores. Regardless, with sealed cases, it’s difficult to blame Best Buy, Walmart , or GameStop for the snafu. The more likely culprits are manufacturing errors that occurred before the game reached storefronts.
The studio is also being criticized again for choosing the code-in-box format. Physical disc supporters already resisted the company's decision to abandon Blu-ray media . Even if a massive file size required an additional download, a disc would still let owners buy and sell the game later. Digital gaming 's convenience isn’t much of an advantage without a way to redeem purchases.
To make matters worse, GTA 6 PS5 and Xbox codes may be at risk of theft by shippers or shoppers . Reports document how a powerful flashlight exposed the sensitive printing without breaking the seal. However, the issue appears localized, with some European boxes lacking the additional protective layer.

articles.title_orig: AI company behind FAA’s SMART tool denies link to ground stop, Duffy confirms
articles.title_zh: AI company behind FAA’s SMART tool denies link to ground stop, Duffy confirms
articles.content_orig:
The US government has expanded the use of an AI tool for advising air traffic controllers to assist in managing air traffic across the entire national airspace system. Airline executives have voiced support for the rollout, but the US labor union representing air traffic controllers has said it was not involved in designing or testing the AI-driven system.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) says the $875 million SMART system has helped reroute 180 flights since being implemented in airspace over Washington, DC, on September 21. The agency claims that this saved an average of 10 minutes per flight and almost 80 gallons of fuel per flight—and it is apparently hoping such results can be replicated nationwide through the expanded deployment.
“After a successful initial rollout to the National Capital Region in September, the FAA will now use SMART in the airspace of all 22 centers across the country to reduce delays, reduce fuel consumption and improve the travel experience for the flying public,” according to the agency statement posted on November 10.
The FAA fact sheet describes SMART as a cloud-based system that combines information about “weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow and controller staffing metrics” to predict air traffic patterns. It is designed to make scheduling recommendations, identify optimal flight routes, and determine the best order of arrivals for aircraft.
However, a human team of FAA specialists based in DC is ultimately responsible for validating the SMART system recommendations before passing them along to air traffic control facilities across the country, according to the agency.
Furthermore, the AI-powered SMART system “cannot be used to replace the critical role air traffic controllers play or take over control of an aircraft,” the FAA clarified in the September 21 announcement about the initial deployment. Local air traffic controllers can decide whether or not to accept the SMART system recommendations.
The previous FAA announcement included supportive statements from Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian and American Airlines CEO Robert Isom.
But the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, which represents more than 15,000 members, also told Flying magazine that it was not consulted or involved in the “design, testing, or implementation of SMART and therefore cannot speak to its effect on the air traffic control workforce.”
Following the initial deployment in airspace above DC, the FAA expanded the SMART system’s coverage to air route traffic control centers in Atlanta along with Jacksonville and Miami in Florida, according to The Dallas Morning News .
The FAA also shared an example with The Dallas Morning News about how SMART recommended a shorter and faster route for a cargo flight arriving at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, although the newspaper noted that the agency did not identify the flight involved and has not provided information about how SMART may have assisted passenger flight traffic.
Ars has previously covered the SMART system’s development and lingering questions about how it works, as well as the air traffic controller shortage and other challenges facing the FAA.

articles.title_orig: Europeans decide on thorny question of who will speak for bloc in Ukraine talks
articles.title_zh: Europeans decide on thorny question of who will speak for bloc in Ukraine talks
articles.content_orig:
European leaders have waited on the margins of negotiations to end Russia’s war in Ukraine for months, eyeing a seat at the table. They learned this week that they would get one, and simply needed to decide which official should sit in that chair.
Instead, they decided on six.
European Union leaders concluded in Dublin on Friday that they will tap a group of major nations — Britain, France, Germany, Poland, and Italy — along with a representative from the E.U’s leadership arms, the European Council and European Commission.
In some ways, the choice of a crowd plays into jibes Americans have made about the continent’s indecisiveness: “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation,” Jared Kushner, President Trump’s son-in-law and a U.S. envoy, said earlier this week.
Europe’s failure to pick one negotiator leaves open the possibility that its fragmentation will diminish its influence. Even so, Europeans have underscored that they are a democracy of many nations and that many voices must be represented.
“We decide on who represents us, and that is what we have done today,” said Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission.
“We need to work as a team,” António Costa, president of the European Union’s political leadership arm, said at a news conference on Friday, noting that America itself has two envoys.

articles.title_orig: US officials raise alarm over restricted Nvidia AI chips reaching China
articles.title_zh: US officials raise alarm over restricted Nvidia AI chips reaching China
articles.content_orig:
President Donald Trump is not expected to raise allegations of a Chinese intelligence operation involving former Nvidia CEO J ensen Huang during his upcoming meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, senior U.S. officials said Friday.
Officials also said that Elon Musk , the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit on Nov. 18 and 19.
The White House, earlier Friday, said Trump plans to have a three-way summit there with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.
"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."
Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."
"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."
China has called the allegations against Alice Huang baseless.
Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed , a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.
The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.
"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

articles.title_orig: Setback for SpaceX reusable rocket system despite successful launch
articles.title_zh: Setback for SpaceX reusable rocket system despite successful launch
articles.content_orig:
US company SpaceX has successfully launched the latest flight of its Starship spacecraft into orbit but did not recover the booster rocket as planned.
The company, owned by tech billionaire Elon Musk , is hoping to develop a fully reusable rocket system. It had planned to recover both the booster and the upper stage, which is the spacecraft itself.
Instead of landing back at the launch site, the booster exploded above the Gulf of Mexico. The upper stage is currently in orbit and the plan is to recover it on Saturday when it returns to Earth.
It is to be caught by mechanical arms upon landing back at the launch pad, marking the first time the spacecraft would be caught after returning to Earth. It could then potentially be reused in the future.
In addition to testing the reusable rocket system, the mission also delivered 26 of SpaceX’s satellites for its Starlink network .
SpaceX's Starship is the world's largest and most powerful rocket system. At 124 meters (407 feet) tall, it consists of a spacecraft mounted on a booster rocket. Both stages were designed from the outset to be fully reusable.
At the launch, both the spacecraft and booster successfully lifted off from the SpaceX South Texas Starbase site. While the Friday launch was an uncrewed mission, Starship is designed to carry both crew and cargo.
On its return path, the booster diverted from its flight path to the launch site and steered to a designated area over the Gulf of Mexico where it exploded over the sea surface. The reasons for the failure of the controlled landing were not immediately clear.
"Not sure right now why we weren't able to bring it back," SpaceX's Dan Huot said.
The upper stage continued into orbit and soon after began releasing the 26 satellites it was carrying.
It is scheduled to return to Earth on Saturday.
Developing a fully reusable rocket system is key to SpaceX’s goal to drive down the cost of spaceflight.
In previous launches, the Starship booster was successfully recovered. The upper stages of the 14 previous Starship missions have all ended up in the ocean though, either by design or because of failures .
The new objective of Friday’s launch was to recover both stages of the Starship launch system.
Currently, SpaceX is mostly using smaller Falcon rockets, which are not fully reusable because the second stage cannot be recovered.
Musk said he expected SpaceX to conduct Starship launches once a week by early 2027.
The project has received billions of dollars in NASA funding, with SpaceX also investing at least $15 billion.
The main goal of the program is to put astronauts on the Moon by 2028 although outstanding technical challenges could delay that schedule.

articles.title_orig: Trump not expected to raise Alice Huang case with China’s Xi, US officials say
articles.title_zh: Trump not expected to raise Alice Huang case with China’s Xi, US officials say
articles.content_orig:
The meeting will be the first between the three leaders.
President Donald Trump will participate in the first-ever trilateral meeting between the leaders of the U.S., China and Russia on the sidelines at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in China next week, senior U.S. officials told reporters Friday evening.
Trump is expected to discuss Iran with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, the officials said, but he does not intend to discuss Russia's war with Ukraine during the trilateral meeting.
Denuclearization will be the focus of the long-awaited trilateral meeting, though officials do not anticipate the leaders reaching any concrete agreement and are characterizing this meeting as an initial conversation broaching the subject.
Trump had been teasing a potential face-to-face meeting with the world's leading nuclear superpowers for some time. On Oct. 19, Trump told ABC News that he would like to meet with Putin and Xi when he visits China, saying, "I would do that," and indicated a desire to discuss denuclearization.
Trump and Xi will meet ahead of their meeting with Putin but Trump and Putin will not be meeting one-on-one separately, the officials said.
Billionaire Elon Musk will be joining Trump for parts of his China travels, the officials said, but did not specify Musk's reason for accompanying the president, merely pointing to his business interests in China.
An official said some additional U.S. business leaders are expected to attend the APEC CEO Summit but clarified that they are not part of the U.S. delegation.
Trump's trip to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC Summit will be his second trip to China this year, as well and his third meeting with Xi . Before the China leg of the trip, Trump will be in Manila for the ASEAN Summit.
There are no plans for a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jung Un while Trump is in Asia, an official added.
The senior U.S. officials said they do not expect the Nvidia controversy of this week to have any impact on the president's trip or his planned meetings after former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned from the tech company over concerns that he had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
Officials said they don't expect Trump to raise with Xi the allegations against Alice Huang, a Chinese national and tech executive at Megaspeed who is accused of being a Chinese spy, adding that the two presidents plan to focus on implementing aspects of their trade agreement.
"You know, I think when it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., it's probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," a senior U.S. official said.
Trump will depart from the White House on Monday morning en route to Manila, where he will participate in a series of multilateral meetings about peace and security in the Indo-Pacific region, the officials said. The president is also expected to sign a trade deal with Thailand, they added.
While in the Philippines, Trump will participate in a welcome ceremony and state visit with Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., followed by a bilateral meeting. Trump is expected to secure "commercial deals and strategic investments" during his two-day visit to the Philippines, officials said.
Trump will then travel to Shenzhen, where he will participate in an APEC leaders' dinner and multilateral meeting with the APEC leaders. On Thursday afternoon, Trump will participate in a bilateral meeting and working lunch with Xi.
The Trump-Xi-Putin meeting will be the final event on the president's Asia trip.

articles.title_orig: SpaceX launches milestone Starship flight to demonstrate full reusability of orbit-class rocket
articles.title_zh: SpaceX launches milestone Starship flight to demonstrate full reusability of orbit-class rocket
articles.content_orig:
In a key test flight on Friday, SpaceX tried but failed to recover both stages of its massive Starship rocket.
The rocket lifted off from the company's South Texas launch facility at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. SpaceX had to abort its plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the Gulf of Mexico, where it burst into flames.
Test Flight 15, the most ambitious Starship mission to date, was the first time Elon Musk's company attempted to catch both the booster and upper stage, or spacecraft portion, of the massive rocket.
Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.
The upper stage of the Starship continued its trajectory into orbit after the company failed to catch and salvage the booster. The rocket is expected to fly around the Earth fourteen times in total. If successful, SpaceX will land the upper stage back at its Starbase facility on Saturday.
Starship's success is critical to SpaceX and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.
The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.
In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 v3 satellites, and released another 26 in the Friday test flight, with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X.
When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential."
Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service.
Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month .
Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX .

articles.title_orig: Trump’s top economic advisers clash over Lutnick’s handling of Nvidia
articles.title_zh: Trump’s top economic advisers clash over Lutnick’s handling of Nvidia
articles.content_orig:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Friday accused the Commerce Department of a delay in labeling Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat, publicly airing an ongoing administration blame game following the ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.
His comments come as some of President Donald Trump’s advisers, reeling from the fallout of Huang’s resignation, have begun discussing whether Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick should be dismissed, according to people familiar with the conversations. Trump himself has also fielded calls from administration officials and outside advisors raising alarm bells about Lutnick, two additional people said.
So far, the White House has stood by him, issuing a statement Thursday – before Bessent’s comments – saying Trump “maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce Secretary in modern history.” Trump and Lutnick are longtime friends, and sources said it was unclear what the president might do.
Speaking on CNBC, Bessent said a wide swath of Trump’s administration — including the Treasury and State departments, the Pentagon and the US Trade Representative — favored placing Megaspeed on an export blacklist.
He said it was the Commerce Department, led by Lutnick, that had failed the follow through.
“Commerce…has the pen. You would have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
He suggested the inaction had violated directives given by Trump.
“I am frustrated when President Trump made it very clear that China should not receive any Nvidia chips above” a certain technological level, he said.
“And so any leakage is very frustrating because it hurts our great companies in the AI race, gives the Chinese an advantage,” he went on.
CNN has reached out to the Commerce Department for comment.
Trump officials have long harbored concerns that Megaspeed has circumvented US law and funneled advanced chips into China — a prospect that Treasury staffers argued should land it on Commerce’s so-called entity list of China-connected companies that could pose national security risks.
But the issue gathered newfound attention and importance in recent days when it was reported publicly that Huang had an affair with a Megaspeed employee suspected of having intelligence connections to China.
Senior Trump officials, including Lutnick, were briefed months ago about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive.
Despite those warnings, Commerce has so far refused to put Megaspeed on the entity list, people familiar with the matter said.
In a tense Situation Room meeting last week, Bessent challenged Lutnick over his department’s reluctance to blacklist Megaspeed, CNN previously reported. Lutnick did not immediately commit to taking any specific action, they said.
In the interview Friday, Bessent did not deny the confrontation .
“We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Do U.S. air traffic control and email blackouts after China AI espionage have a common answer?
articles.title_zh: Do U.S. air traffic control and email blackouts after China AI espionage have a common answer?
articles.content_orig:
An old English proverb anchored in superstition from ancient Greek and Roman beliefs is that bad luck always comes in threes, but that does not mean bad luck was always random.
The United States has now experienced two debilitating, unprecedented blackouts across critical infrastructure in two days. The timing is almost too coincidental to be a coincidence – coming on the heels of the removal of Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO amidst an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, widespread recriminations about chip exports to China, and demands for tighter export controls and more hawkish policies against China.
Could China and other hostile foreign actors be targeting U.S. infrastructure? It’s too early to know for sure, but the country deserves far more transparent answers than we have received so far.
At 3:54 p.m. ET on Friday , November 13, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded every departing flight in America, “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” It was only the third nationwide ground stop ever ordered. The first came on Sept. 11, 2001; the second more than 20 years later, on Jan. 11, 2023.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy would say only that “a communication issue” had struck every one of the 22 centers that guide planes across the country, and that technicians were investigating. A subsequent press conference by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin did little to reassure anyone, with no answers about what happened and little reassurance that it would be fixable anytime soon, with airports sending travelers home and communicating that flight cancellations would persist for many hours at a minimum, if not days.
It was the second time in two days that critical infrastructure the country cannot function without simply stopped, potentially for very nefarious reasons. The day before, Microsoft’s Outlook, Teams and Copilot went dark in 74 countries and stayed down for hours. Both blackouts struck within a day-and-a-half of the most damaging China espionage story in years.
The last nationwide ground stop, in 2023, lasted about 90 minutes and still delayed more than 10,000 flights and canceled 1,300 . Friday’s lasted hours with no resolution imminent on the horizon. At the four-hour point of this latest ground stop, 10,243 flights were already delayed and 3,234 cancelled, with flights grounded not only at single regional airports but across the entire nation, suggesting systemic breakdowns rather than localized issues.
Microsoft’s failure began at 11:17 a.m. ET on Thursday and spread across 19 Microsoft 365 services . Within an hour, complaints about Outlook were running at more than 2,000 times their normal level . Microsoft counts more than 450 million paid commercial seats , with many millions of those users locked out entirely from their inboxes and other critical services.
The casualty list reads like a roll call of essential services: the U.S. House of Representatives was substantively incapacitated; a federal appeals court that could not send or receive email; Britain’s Parliament and its National Health Service, where the failure threatened patients’ prescriptions; Australia’s spy agency and federal police were sent offline as well.
When a botched CrowdStrike update crashed 8.5 million machines in 2024, the Fortune 500 alone lost an estimated $5.4 billion . One risk adviser already puts Microsoft’s bill in the billions for Australia alone , not to mention the lost economic value in the U.S. or the rest of the world. This was the first time in history so many users were locked out for so long – with shifting and unsatisfactory explanations. Similarly, this is the first time in global aviation history where there has been a nationwide ground stop with no satisfactory, clear explanation and immediate fix.
Microsoft wrote the playbook for false comfort. For a full day it insisted there was “no indication” of malicious activity while its own bulletins showed it did not know what had broken. If it did not know for sure, then how could they know for sure there was no indication of anything malicious amidst shifting explanations?
First it blamed elevated load, then servers that had unexpectedly dropped out . It found no recent change that lined up with the failure. Hours later, it was rolling back a network change that did . Early Friday, engineers were still trying to “pinpoint the underlying cause of the traffic influx.”
Only on Friday afternoon did Microsoft name a culprit : a flaw introduced during a network capacity upgrade, “not related to cyber.” That sequence is as nonsensical as it is falsely reassuring. No patient would trust a doctor who swears it is not an infection before he can diagnose the fever. You cannot rule out what you cannot yet explain, and nobody can feel particularly reassured from this disturbing sequence of events and shifting explanations.
On Thursday morning, Nvidia, whose board failures we dissected in Fortune this week , announced the resignation of Jensen Huang , the chip industry’s loudest advocate for selling to China, after he admitted an affair with a businesswoman U.S. officials suspect of spying for Beijing . Beijing has been vocal in calling it a smear amidst a rapid escalation of U.S.-China tensions. Lawmakers in both parties are demanding testimony and tighter export controls . Within three hours, inboxes went dark from Capitol Hill to Canberra. A day later, planes stopped and were grounded.
Could that really be a coincidence?
Perhaps we are being too conspiratorial, but there is a certain uncanny resemblance to Beijing’s favorite playbook, which is to divert from negative news stories by shutting down internet services and diverting public attention.
For example, in 2011, a petition to free Ai Weiwei got Change.org knocked offline . In 2012, exposés of the family fortunes of Xi Jinping and Wen Jiabao got Bloomberg and The New York Times blocked in China and targeted by hackers . In 2014, as Hong Kong marched for democracy, a newspaper and a voting site were buried under one of the largest attacks the internet had ever seen . In 2015, China’s “Great Cannon” hammered GitHub for days for hosting banned news. In 2019, Telegram and the LIHKG forum were swamped as Hong Kong marched again. In 2022, news of the zero-COVID protests on Twitter drowned in a deluge of spam . Maybe this pattern of untimely hacks was merely a coincidence – or could it have been more than coincidence?
Microsoft knows this adversary better than anyone. Hackers tied to Beijing tore through its customers’ Exchange servers in 2021 and stole some 60,000 State Department emails through its cloud in 2023, a breach a federal review board blamed on a “cascade of security failures” at Microsoft. Just three weeks ago, Microsoft itself said a China-aligned group had turned AI agents loose on more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 customers .
Whatever the cause, the lesson is identical. Some cyber experts are warning about potentially economically destabilizing cyberattacks, with researchers warning that AI-enabled hacking is spreading like a virus: attacks on previously unknown flaws have roughly doubled since capable open-source models arrived.
U.S. agencies say China’s Volt Typhoon hackers have already burrowed into American communications, transportation, energy and water networks , in some cases for five years, positioning themselves to disrupt them. They sat inside one small Massachusetts electric and water utility for more than 300 days . If the inbox and the skies can go dark on consecutive days, why not the grid, or the tap? Is it time for every business and household to buy storage batteries, water tanks, MREs and porta potties?
Of course, regardless of whether this was a Chinese or foreign malevolent actor attack, or whether it was merely the coincidental degradation of antiquated and outdated infrastructure systems, all of this takes place against the backdrop of the substantive hollowing out of U.S. government cou

articles.title_orig: Silicon Valley plots Jensen Huang’s comeback
articles.title_zh: Silicon Valley plots Jensen Huang’s comeback
articles.content_orig:
In a matter of days, a corporate scandal has toppled the leader of the world’s second-most valuable company, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang; thrust his family into the spotlight; raised huge questions about the future of the AI industry; and landed on Washington’s doorstep.
Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday morning in the wake of mounting scrutiny following reports of multiple extramarital relationships, including one with Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman and former executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed whom US officials had been investigating as a potential national security risk.
Nvidia’s board named longtime CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. Investors and Wall Street analysts are likely to have big questions for her when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday.
In the meantime, Jensen Huang and some key members of the Trump administration are facing questions from lawmakers about the sales and transfer of Nvidia chips to China.
Huang has been called to testify in a closed-door congressional hearing on December 1; lawmakers have said they will subpoena him if he doesn’t voluntarily agree to testify. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify next month before the Senate Banking Committee, which has also requested to hear from Huang.
Huang’s resignation represents a rapid and stunning fall from grace for one of the most powerful men in tech. Huang had run and largely been synonymous with Nvidia in the 33 years since he cofounded it in a Denny’s restaurant in 1993.
His Thursday exit was a marked reversal from just days earlier. On Sunday, the Nvidia board said it would investigate whether Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, but expressed confidence in his leadership and said it did not believe company secrets or national security had been compromised. The same day, Huang admitted to an extramarital affair, but did not name the other party.
But in the subsequent days, growing national security concerns on Capitol Hill — as well as reports that Huang had at least one additional extramarital relationship — appeared to force the board’s hand.
It convened Wednesday night to weigh Huang’s future, and he was out the next morning.
Nvidia’s stock ( NVDA ) has taken a beating amid the scandal. As of Friday’s close, Nvidia’s shares had fallen 12.75% since the start of the week, erasing roughly $573 billion in market value.
That has wider implications beyond just the company and its investors.
Nvidia is one of the largest stocks in the S&P 500 — it comprises about 6% of the total value of the index — meaning its decline has broad implications for many people’s investment and retirement accounts.
CNN’s John Towfighi and Rosa de Acosta contributed reporting.
